documents.abstract: Abstract Command and control (C2) is an agile crisis management architecture for highly uncertain emergencies, originating from military operations but now widely deployed in public safety emergency response, traffic and airspace management, industrial energy systems, urban governance, and large-scale event coordination. Traditional C2 systems mainly rely on preset rules, static processes and manual decision-making, which expose obvious limitations in the face of modern environments with high dynamics, complex disturbances and incomplete information. Aiming at the significant problems of traditional command and control systems, such as structural rigidity, information overload, decision lag, and insufficient collaboration, based on the concepts of software factory and single-agent factory, combined with the latest progress of large-small model collaboration in the field of command and control, this paper proposes a new paradigm of large-small model collaboration empowering command and control—the concept of C2 multi-agent factory, which upgrades the single-agent factory that produces “individual intelligence” to a multi-agent factory that produces and runs “swarm intelligence”, and is combined with the command and control system and its application scenarios. The overall system architecture of the C2 multi-agent factory and the large-small model collaboration mechanism based on the C2 multi-agent factory are given. Finally, an application example is given to further illustrate how the C2 multi-agent factory can use the large-small model collaboration technology to empower command and control. The C2 multi-agent factory proposed in this paper will find a new path for the construction of an evolvable intelligent command and control system, promote the substantive leap of artificial intelligence towards the C2 system.

Explanations of LLM outputs are considered an important way to make model behavior legible, helping human users make good decisions on downstream tasks. However, default training approaches for improving explanations target model task performance or human preference rather than human decision quality. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{HD-RL}, a reinforcement learning framework for optimizing LLM explanations for human decision making. Our approach calibrates a human decision simulator on observed human decisions, applying a proxy reward model to optimize the LLM to generate explanations that help people to make good decisions. We apply this framework to AI-generated text detection. In our initial data collection phase, we observed that while LLMs possess strong autonomous detection capabilities, the explanations they generate for users yield near-random human accuracy (51.3\%). By applying the HD-RL framework to the open-source Qwen 3.6 model, we generate optimized explanations that improve human performance, achieving a GLMM-estimated human accuracy of 63.7\% in a randomized between-subjects experiment with repeated measures and outperforming RLVR, RLAIF, and other baselines by over 8\%.

Most classrooms still move at one speed. A teacher with thirty or forty students has to choose a pace that suits the middle of the class, which leaves weaker students behind and keeps stronger students waiting. AI-based adaptive learning systems promise to change this by watching how each student answers, estimating what that student already knows, and choosing the next task to match. This paper examines how far that promise holds for senior school students. It explains how adaptive systems work in simple terms, reviews findings from major meta-analyses and field experiments, including a randomised study of the Mindspark program in Delhi, and compares adaptive learning with the traditional one-size-fits-all approach. The evidence suggests that well-designed adaptive systems produce real and sometimes large learning gains, with reported effect sizes between about 0.2 and 0.8 standard deviations, and that students who are furthest behind often gain the most. However, the gains depend heavily on how the system is designed and how it is used. Systems that simply give answers can weaken learning, and results shrink when teachers are not involved. The paper concludes that AI can personalise practice, feedback and pacing to a significant extent, but it cannot replace the motivational, social and judgement-based work of a teacher. A blended model, in which AI handles adaptive practice and teachers use the data to guide instruction, is proposed for Indian senior schools.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study examines how cognitive and affective factors drive Vietnamese transnational education (TNE) students' intention to use ChatGPT for English academic writing, and investigates how information verification and responsible use enhance English writing proficiency (EWP). Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 501 TNE students across three major Vietnamese cities were analysed using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling. The conceptual model integrates the technology acceptance model, the pupils’ attitudes toward technology short questionnaire (PATT-SQ) model and Mitcham’s philosophical framework. Insights from an expert survey of six lecturers supported the interpretation and practical implications. Findings Cognitive factors (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use and perceived risk) significantly influence ChatGPT usage intention, whereas affective factors do not. Perceived risk negatively impacts intention, reflecting student awareness of potential drawbacks. The results further reveal a strong behavioural pathway in which frequent use intention promotes information verification, which fosters responsible use and ultimately improves EWP. This demonstrates that learning outcomes depend on critical, ethical engagement rather than usage frequency alone. Research limitations/implications Higher education institutions (HEI) should embed AI literacy, verification practices and ethical guidelines into curricula to optimise ChatGPT utility and mitigate dependency. Limitations include a cross-sectional design, lack of contextual factors and a localised sample, which future longitudinal and comparative studies should address. Originality/value This study offers one of the first empirical examinations linking ChatGPT adoption, verification behaviours, responsible use and measurable EWP gains among Vietnamese TNE students. By integrating cognitive, affective, behavioural and ethical dimensions, it extends traditional technology adoption models to the context of generative AI-assisted academic writing.

documents.abstract: The first industrial robot, the PUMA (Programmable Universal Manipulator Arm) was built by a company called animation in 1961. According to history, 50 years ago robots were viewed as creations designed to exterminate the human race as portrayed in science fictions. To help resolve this assumption, Isaac Asimov compounded the three laws of robotics to protect humans from interactions with robots (Asimov 1984). The laws states that: (1) a robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm. (2) a robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law. (3) a robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Laws. (1). Asimov’s law are considered unscientific by researchers yet it unarguably forms the basis of various machine learning activities used in many manufacturing sectors. Furthermore, the field of robotics has highly evolved by producing a wide variety of objects from autonomous machines to human collaborative robots through the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning. By monitoring the ever increasing research activities in machine learning, it cannot be denied that human robot collaborations is only expected to keep growing. In the logistics industry, collaborative robots are achieving human-like dexterity which allows for increased productivity. This work expands on the foundation of existing scientific research in the ergonomic aspect of human robot communication in warehouses which promotes seamless collaboration of robots and human workers.

This study examines the effect of Midjourney and DALLE-3, artificial intelligence-based visual production programs, on the creative thinking and artistic expression levels of art teacher candidates. The research was conducted with experimental and control groups consisting of ten students enrolled in the Art Education program at Sivas Cumhuriyet University. The experimental group produced traditional charcoal drawings, while the control group produced AI-assisted charcoal drawings. Data were collected through qualitative comparative analysis and quantitative surveys, analyzed using SPSS, and the similarities and differences between the two approaches were evaluated. The findings obtained within the scope of the research show that manual charcoal applications have a stronger impact on students' artistic expression depth, aesthetic decision-making processes, and experience-based learning gains than artificial intelligence programs. It has been determined that traditional techniques provide a holistic contribution, especially in terms of tactile feedback, error, tolerance process, and individual application process. In contrast, AI-supported production programs were found to offer distinct advantages in terms of technical accuracy, time management, alternative composition generation, and visual variation development. In this context, AI applications were observed to accelerate the creative process and provide technical support. The results, based on the findings, indicate that AI-based visual production programs are complementary tools rather than replacements for traditional art education.

Language models are often evaluated alone but increasingly deployed together, routed between, made to debate, ensembled, or collaboratively trained. For a model inside a system, what matters most is not how well it performs on its own, but how much the system gains from its presence. We call this a model's compositional strength and formalize it using the Shapley value of a cooperative game over coalitions of a model pool, and use a model's leave-one-out contribution to the full coalition as a tractable proxy, requiring n+1 rather than 2^n system evaluations. Evaluating individual vs. compositional strengths across five model pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets, we find them largely uncorrelated: in 12 of 15 (pool, method-family) settings, individual strength does not translate into compositional advantages, and the coupling is weakest among general-purpose models that practitioners are most likely to deploy. Standalone benchmarks are therefore often poor proxies for models' value in collaborative systems. We then propose compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL), which trains a policy inside a live multi-model system and rewards the outcome produced by the system as a whole, rather than the policy's correctness in isolation. The leave-one-out baseline in Shapley values cancels under a group policy gradient, so this needs no additional rollout cost beyond RL on the collaborative system's outcome and never requires running a coalition without the policy. Across three collaboration protocols and eight tasks spanning reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery, C-RL produces the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings, lifting collaborative performance by +4.0 to +5.4 pts on average (~3x the gain of baselines), up to +13.1 pts.

The rapid deployment of agentic AI has introduced complex challenges for the ethics and governance of AI systems. Agents built on large language models act through tools on behalf of people, and each deployment case brings its own instructions, policies, evidence, and stakeholders, so alignment must be formed case by case. To this end, this work proposes agentic reflective equilibrium (ARE), a computational reflective equilibrium framework that serves as an ethical alignment scaffold in the agent harness. Drawing inspiration from the reflective equilibrium of John Rawls, the scaffold links principles from the system prompt and operator policy, considered judgments, tool evidence, and candidate actions through typed support and attack relations, with provenance encoding the instruction hierarchy. The agent acts on an equilibrium of this state and calls tools or asks questions only while doing so is worth its cost, unless a due-diligence mandate requires them. Governance enters through value priorities, source authority, prohibitions, human-in-the-loop triggers, and mandates, and certificates attribute each action to the sources whose commitments drove it. We show that equilibria are Nash equilibria of a mutual-adjustment game and establish monotonicity, lexical priority, stability certificates, and a quarantine theorem for prompt injection. Two case studies illustrate the framework: a computer-use assistant told to win a refund "whatever it takes" files an honest warranty claim, refuses a fake review, and ignores an injected request for personal data; a hiring agent showcases how authority, oversight triggers, audit mandates, and hard prohibitions shape discrimination, privacy violations, and escalation. The framework offers traceability, coherence, and adaptivity, facilitating safe, secure, and trustworthy agentic AI.

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Health economic models (HEMs) are crucial for assessing the cost-effectiveness of healthcare interventions, informing policy decisions and guiding reimbursement strategies. This study examines the feasibility of employing generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) for the conceptualisation of HEMs. Two proof-of-concept studies were conducted, implementing a first-of-its-kind agentic Gen-AI-augmented approach for model conceptualisation. METHODS: An agentic Gen-AI framework was developed, incorporating the chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning algorithm through advanced prompt engineering, compounded with self-consistency, executed in an external Python programming environment. Within this framework, an agentic execution layer (the 'agent') autonomously orchestrated a multi-step retrieval-reasoning-generation task. Additionally, a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) technique was implemented by linking the large language model (LLM) to an external database curated with user-selected data specific to HEM. Two case studies were explored: breast cancer, representing a data-rich disease area, and transthyretin amyloid polyneuropathy (ATTR-PN), exemplifying a data-sparse rare disease. RESULTS: The agentic Gen-AI framework successfully generated two key outputs that were subsequently validated against published literature and expert review from health economic (HE) modelers and clinicians: (1) a disease concept diagram illustrating the progression of the disease and its associated health states, and (2) a model structure diagram depicting patient transitions between various health states. CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that Gen-AI-augmented methodologies can enhance multiple aspects of HEM conceptualisation, including problem definition, disease and treatment effect pathway development, model structure recommendations, and drafting of model specification plans. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to integrate cutting-edge Gen-AI techniques such as human-in-the-loop (HITL), chain of thought-self-consistency (CoT-SC), and graph-based RAG for HEM conceptualisation or broader health economics and outcomes research (HEOR) applications.

documents.abstract: Software agents built on large language models act by issuing tool calls, some of which cannot be undone. To control theory the model is an opaque feedback controller, replaced every few months, whose closed loop cannot be analyzed directly. We propose a runtime filter, or shield, between any such controller and its environment that certifies a bound on the probability of reaching an unsafe condition during a bounded task. Given a predicate abstraction and candidate successor sets, everything else comes from logs: the loop becomes a finite controlled Markov chain, the estimated kernel is surrounded by a distribution-free confidence region, and robust reach-avoid value iteration runs over it. The certificate is probably approximately correct and uniform over controllers respecting the filter, so one model may replace another without recomputation. In all tested datasets the true risk stayed within certificate and budget; in a file-system sandbox the filter stays sound against a hazard the logs barely covered, where a plug-in baseline certifies safety and fails; and it holds seven controllers, three of them open-weights models, to zero unsafe outcomes in 1050 episodes.

Objective Guided by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a conceptual framework, this study explored medical students’ use of large language models (LLMs) in graduation thesis writing, focusing on application patterns, perceptions, and potential risks. Methods A comparative cross-sectional questionnaire survey using convenience sampling was conducted among medical graduates from medical schools in China in 2024 and 2025. The self-designed 25-item questionnaire included five-point Likert items on perceived advantages and disadvantages of LLMs. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's α , exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was performed, and univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to identify factors associated with LLMs use. Results A total of 341 valid questionnaires were collected. Overall, 54.25% (185/341) of respondents reported using LLMs in graduation thesis writing, with use reported by 27.37% (52/190) in 2024 and 88.08% (133/151) in 2025. ChatGPT was the most frequently used platform in 2024 (82.69%, 43/52), whereas Deepseek was the most frequently used platform in 2025 (88.72%, 118/133). LLMs were used primarily during the literature review stage (74.05%, 137/185), mainly to provide writing suggestions (82.16%, 152/185). Cronbach's α was 0.720 for perceived advantages and 0.650 for perceived disadvantages, and exploratory factor analysis identified a two-factor clustering pattern consistent with the predefined grouping of perceived advantages and disadvantages. Among LLMs users, 68.65% (127/185) believed that LLMs use would not compromise academic integrity, whereas 47.57% (88/185) remained concerned about potential academic misconduct. The main perceived disadvantages included the risk of academic misconduct, limited content accuracy, and data privacy and security concerns. The findings were discussed with reference to TAM-related concepts as an interpretive framework. Conclusion LLMs use was substantially higher in the 2025 survey than in the 2024 survey. Although LLMs improve writing efficiency and provide valuable writing support, concerns regarding academic integrity, content accuracy, and data privacy remain important considerations. The TAM provides a useful framework for interpreting students’ adoption patterns and may inform the development of AI education and governance strategies in medical education.

documents.abstract: Enterprise generative artificial intelligence assistants can retrieve organizational information, recommend decisions, and initiate actions through connected tools. These capabilities make cybersecurity a question of how authority and responsibility are distributed across systems and organizations. This study examines how public guidance translates security responsibilities into controls over enterprise AI assistants. A purposive corpus of 12 documentary units from public bodies, a security community, and technology providers was retrieved on 28 September 2026. Focused qualitative document analysis combined six initial coding categories with cross-document comparison, producing a register of 27 evidence records. Four interpretive themes were developed: responsibility is allocated at different organizational and technical levels; permission inheritance requires contextual judgment about appropriate access; human oversight depends on enforceable intervention points; and incident accountability requires continuity across organizational and temporal boundaries. Counterevidence matters: the corpus contains explicit oversight, authorization, and incident-management provisions, so it does not support a general claim that AI security guidance lacks responsibility requirements. The analysis instead identifies an implementation translation problem between broad obligations, application-level controls, and locally assigned decision rights. A proposed governance framework links retrieval, recommendation, and action capabilities to permission boundaries, intervention conditions, accountable owners, and retained decision evidence. The framework is an analytical synthesis, not an empirically validated maturity model. The study contributes a focused account of responsibility at transitions between AI capabilities and offers an auditable structure for enterprise deployment decisions. Its conclusions concern the selected documents and do not establish organizational compliance, control effectiveness, or industry-wide prevalence.

documents.abstract: Executive Summary Serbia’s artificial intelligence (AI) landscape is evolving rapidly. It is being shaped by parallel advances in digitalisation, innovation, industrial adoption and emerging regulatory frameworks. In recent years, the country has invested in modernising public services, strengthening its research and innovation capacity, and supporting the growth of high-tech companies and start-ups. These developments have created a foundation for the more systematic and large-scale deployment of AI across key sectors, including Health, Energy, Environment & Sustainability, and Culture & Language domains, where growing technological capabilities and a progressively more mature ecosystem can be developed. The primary objective of this report is to establish an empirical and analytical foundation for positioning Serbian Artificial Intelligence Factory Antenna (SAIFA) as the central national mechanism for integrating the Serbian AI ecosystem into the wider European high-performance computing (Europa) value chain. In strict alignment with the project proposal's description, the deliverable provides a detailed mapping of Serbian AI ecosystem actors, business domains, regulatory drivers, and barriers to adoption, alongside a dedicated focus on four priority verticals: Health, Energy, Environment & Sustainability, and Culture & Language. The report is structured to provide a comprehensive assessment of Serbia’s emerging AI ecosystem, combining desk-based analysis with planned field research. It first presents the methodology applied throughout the assessment, including the main analytical approaches, data sources and criteria used for mapping and evaluating the national AI landscape. The subsequent sections present the findings of the desktop research, including an assessment of the Serbian AI landscape and an analysis of stakeholders relevant to the SAIFA project. The AI landscape assessment covers four key dimensions of the national AI ecosystem: research & education, industry & commercial AI activities, regulatory framework, and computational infrastructure. The stakeholder analysis, in turn, identifies the organization’s and stakeholder groups relevant to SAIFA, examining their roles, capabilities, needs and potential contribution to the project and its activities. Starting in September 2026, the assessment will be complemented by field research involving interviews, surveys and focus groups with different stakeholder groups. This research will provide a more in-depth understanding of the barriers, needs, opportunities and potential for AI development and adoption in Serbia, complementing the evidence gathered through the desktop analysis. The findings from the field research will subsequently be consolidated and disseminated through dedicated thematic SAIFA White Papers, providing evidence-based insights into AI readiness, adoption barriers, user needs and development opportunities in selected areas. The results will also be formally incorporated into Deliverable D2.3, ensuring that the evidence collected through field research feeds directly into the subsequent stages of the SAIFA project. The entire research architecture is designed to remain coherent with international benchmarks and the engagement models of sister European AI Factories, specifically Pharos and IT4LIA, while ensuring strict compliance with General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and data management protocols. Alongside this report, a structured Serbian AI Ecosystem Database was developed, providing a tabular overview of AI-related scientific and research projects, publications by authors affiliated with Serbian institutions, patent applications, study programmes, AI companies, ecosystem enablers, support programmes, regulatory frameworks and regulatory-development initiatives, public institutions, and national AI and computing infrastructure. The database is designed to be made publicly accessible through the SAIFA website and to serve as a living resource that can be regularly updated as the Serbian AI ecosystem evolves. The assessment of macroeconomic and general digital preconditions positions Serbia as a fast-advancing adopter and the leading Western Balkan (WB) economy in AI readiness. This trajectory is underpinned by a highly competitive Information and Communications Technology (ICT) sector, which achieved a record export surplus and an all-time high total export value of €4.55 billion in 2025 (OITEG, 2026). However, a granular evaluation across the four conceptual pillars of the AI ecosystem reveals deep structural asymmetries: · Research, Innovation and Education: Serbia has introduced foundational AI components across primary and secondary curricula and accredited nine specialized AI-focused degree programs since 2021. Scientific publication output has experienced a sharp expansion, exceeding 450 AI-related papers in 2025. Conversely, the commercialization of this knowledge remains a critical bottleneck; only 66 AI-related patent applications were filed between 2017 and mid-2026, highlighting a weak technology-transfer pipeline from academia to market. · Industry and Firm-Level Intensity: The domestic AI business landscape comprises approximately 300 developers and integrators. Startups and Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SMEs) form the dominant core, accounting for 89% of these firms, showcasing high agility and an entrepreneurial drive that culminated in the emergence of Serbia’s first tech unicorn (Ominimo) in 2026. However, the corporate and venture capital layers are thin. Venture capital (VC) expenditure stands at a critical low of 8.0% of the EU average, leaving the startup base heavily reliant on public grants and personal funds, which severely restricts their ability to scale commercially. · Regulation and Governance: Serbia has actively established strategic policy intent, moving from its initial Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia (SDAIRS) (2020–2025) and Ethical Guidelines to a comprehensive new SDAIRS for the Period 2025–2030. In the absence of specialized legislation, AI is currently governed by a distributed matrix of horizontal laws (data protection, cybersecurity, non-discrimination). The upcoming draft Law on Artificial Intelligence, largely aligned with the EU AI Act, signals Serbia’s move towards a more comprehensive AI regulatory framework. · Computational Infrastructure: Serbia’s computational infrastructure is developing rapidly, with significant investments in national AI and High-Performance Computing (HPC) capacity. Hosted at the Government Data Center in Kragujevac (GDCK), the National AI Platform has reached a combined operational capacity of 37 PFLOPS using NVIDIA A100 and H200 GPU architectures. The planned delivery of a third supercomputer based on NVIDIA Grace Hopper technology in early 2027 will further strengthen Serbia’s national AI and computing capacity. This report also provides a systematic Stakeholder Analysis, categorising ecosystem actors according to their functional roles within the AI ecosystem. The analysis distinguishes four main groups: Data Providers and Domain Experts (public institutions, utilities and industrial organisations holding valuable datasets and domain knowledge), AI Researchers and Model Developers (universities and research institutes providing methodological and machine-learning expertise), AI Application Developers (startups and software companies turning AI capabilities into applications), and End-Users and Beneficiaries (e.g. patients, farmers, businesses and public administrations whose needs define the objectives of AI solutions). The analysis is complemented by cross-cutting ecosystem enablers and intermediaries, including science and technology parks, industry associations, chambers, incubators and accelerators, as well as investors, funding organisations and public authorities. Their role is particularly important for matchmaking, dissemination, funding, regulation and creating the conditions for collaboration. Sector-specific analyses were conducted for healthcare, energy, environment & sustainability, and language & culture, identifying relevant stakeholder groups, concrete organisations, and the resources they can contribute or require. Illustrative use cases, presented in this section, demonstrate how organisations with complementary data, domain expertise, AI capabilities and market access can be connected through SAIFA. The analysis therefore proposes stakeholder engagement activities focused on turning connections into concrete projects, including thematic workshops and roundtables, AI-focused forums and hackathons, direct outreach and bilateral meetings, SAIFA information sessions, and participation in sector-specific and scientific events. Together, these activities position SAIFA not only as an AI and HPC service provider, but as a facilitator of collaboration, resource exchange and joint solution development across Serbia’s AI ecosystem. Serbia’s strongest AI potential lies in HealthTech and BioTech, as well as in environment and sustainability, where established research capacities, relevant data, industry demand and an emerging base of technology providers provide a solid foundation for further development. At the same time, culture & language, as well as cybersecurity, represent emerging high-potential areas, characterised by a growing number of AI-related projects, research activities and companies, although their ecosystem bases are currently less developed. These areas therefore offer significant opportunities for targeted ecosystem-building and are particularly relevant to SAIFA’s project priorities. The ecosystem is geographically concentrated around Belgrade, Novi Sad, Niš and Kragujevac, with major Research and Development (R&D) and computing capacities centred on leading universities, research institutes and national infrastructure. The deep learning approach in education is a learning strategy oriented toward in-depth conceptual understanding, reflection, and integration of knowledge. This study aims to analyze the deep learning approach from the perspectives of multiple learning theories, namely behaviorism, cognitivism, humanism, and constructivism. The deep learning approach is considered relevant to addressing the challenges of twenty-first-century education because it emphasizes deep conceptual understanding, critical thinking skills, and learners’ active engagement in the learning process. However, the implementation of this approach is often not supported by a strong theoretical understanding. Therefore, this study employs a descriptive qualitative literature review method by analyzing various academic sources to identify the contributions of each learning theory to the deep learning approach. The findings indicate that behaviorism shapes purposeful learning behaviors; cognitivism provides a foundation for information-processing strategies and metacognition; humanism emphasizes the importance of intrinsic motivation, personal values, and individual growth; while constructivism supports active, collaborative, and contextualized learning. The synthesis of these four perspectives establishes a comprehensive conceptual foundation for developing transformative and holistic deep learning instructional designs. This study makes a significant conceptual contribution to the development of learning strategies that integrate behavioral, cognitive, affective, and social dimensions in a balanced manner.

Purpose: This article develops a Human Governed Agentic Project Management (HG-APM) model for integrating autonomous AI capabilities with human project management authority. Design/methodology/approach: An integrative conceptual synthesis combines four literature streams: AI-enabled project management, autonomous Manager Agents, human oversight governance, and human–AI teaming. Source supported findings are separated from conceptual inferences, and the resulting architecture is expressed as a closed-loop model. Findings: The model comprises Sense, Understand, Diagnose, Predict, Plan, Evaluate, Authorize, Act, Monitor, Learn and Replan. It proposes a consequence sensitive, graduated autonomy rather than a single autonomy level. Routine and reversible actions may be automated within predefined boundaries, whereas consequential financial, contractual, scope, safety, stakeholder, reputational and strategic decisions require stronger authority from the designated human or organizational decisionmaker. Originality: The model integrates project-management intelligence, human–AI teaming and governance into one operational architecture. It contributes to a project specific decision boundary and testable propositions for evaluating whether governed agentic AI improves project outcomes without weakening human control.

Digital transformation in healthcare, driven by the widespread adoption of electronic health records, the growth of large-scale health data, the expansion of telehealth applications, and advances in data-processing capacity, is strengthening the role of artificial intelligence within healthcare systems. Technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and generative artificial intelligence are increasingly used in diagnosis and screening, clinical decision support, personalized care, patient monitoring, workflow optimization, and the improvement of access to healthcare services. This chapter provides a comprehensive conceptual and narrative review of the effects of artificial intelligence on healthcare services and health economics. It examines the impact of AI on diagnostic accuracy, early detection, clinical decision-making, healthcare professionals’ workload, service capacity, workforce productivity, access, and equity. In addition, the economic value of AI applications is evaluated in terms of cost-effectiveness, cost-benefit, resource allocation, reimbursement mechanisms, health technology assessment, and implementation costs. Existing evidence indicates that AI can accelerate diagnostic processes, reduce unnecessary procedures and tests, improve the utilization of healthcare professionals and high-cost medical equipment, and generate cost-effective outcomes in specific applications. However, the economic value of AI is not uniform across healthcare systems or areas of application. Patient volume, workforce costs, existing infrastructure, licensing and integration expenses, maintenance and updating costs, reimbursement structures, and institutional characteristics of healthcare systems substantially influence economic outcomes. Ethical and regulatory issues, including data security, algorithmic bias, explainability, clinical accountability, human oversight, and equity in access to healthcare, are also critical to the sustainable adoption of AI technologies. Overall, the value of artificial intelligence in healthcare should not be assessed solely on the basis of technical performance or short-term cost savings. A comprehensive assessment should consider clinical outcomes, economic value, implementation conditions, human–AI collaboration, ethical responsibilities, and long-term sustainability together.

documents.abstract: Against the backdrop of the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence technologies, traditional design value assessment systems based on creative input are facing new challenges. This study aims to examine the effects of design source (human-designed design vs. AI-assisted design), design style (commercial style vs. AI-native style), and campaign duration on the value assessment of design works in the AI era. Drawing on a real e-commerce platform context, the study conducts empirical analyses through two multifactor experiments. Experiment 1 adopts a 2 × 5 mixed experimental design to compare the value assessment performance of human-designed and AI-assisted design works across different campaign durations. Experiment 2 further introduces the variable of design style and employs a 2 × 2 × 5 three-factor experimental design to investigate the interaction effects among design source, design style, and campaign duration. The findings indicate that AI-assisted design demonstrates significant efficiency advantages in terms of time and cost. However, regarding value assessment indicators such as number of clicks, click-through rate (CTR), conversion rate (CVR), and sales performance, AI-assisted design performs comparably to human-designed design overall. Different design styles exhibit stage-specific differences: commercial style is more effective in attracting user attention and promoting conversion during the early stage of campaigns, whereas AI-native style gradually demonstrates higher conversion efficiency and cost advantages in the middle and later stages. In addition, the value assessment of design works exhibits significant temporal dynamics, with advertising performance reaching a relatively optimal level during the middle stage of campaign deployment. The study finds that AI significantly reduces creative input without weakening the market performance of design works, providing new evidence for understanding the input–outcome relationship in design value. The study also offers practical insights for enterprises seeking to optimize collaborative creation strategies between AI and human designers. Training LLM agents to interact with users over multiple turns is challenging because the learning signal depends not only on the agent, but also on the user simulator and environment, which jointly shape the agent's experience. Simulated users can be stochastic or inconsistent, while environments may contain unreliable tools, incomplete state coverage, and incorrect verifiers. Prior work mainly addresses the resulting instability through reward shaping or denser supervision, while treating these components as fixed. We instead introduce EAU, a meta-agent framework for environment--agent--user co-evolution. During training, EAU monitors trajectories, tool traces, rewards, and training statistics; diagnoses failures and uninformative interactions; and proposes targeted modifications to the user simulator, environment, reward design, and RL configuration. Validated changes are hot-swapped into the ongoing run, allowing the training setup to evolve together with the policy. These adaptations also persist across runs, so later training can build on previously discovered improvements rather than restarting from a fixed setup. We enable this process through an editable symbolic representation of user and environment dynamics, while the agent remains a neural LLM optimized with RL. Across three interactive-agent benchmarks and two backbone models, EAU consistently outperforms prior RL methods, improving the overall score over the strongest baseline by 14.7--15.0% and increasing successful task completion on ColBench by up to 36.7%, showing that co-evolving the training system with the policy can substantially improve multi-turn RL.

This systematic review evaluates the effectiveness, diagnostic accuracy, and implementation outcomes of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted screening tools for depression and anxiety in primary care settings, with a focus on literature published since the advent of advanced large language models. …

documents.abstract: Abstract With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), AI-assisted tools are increasingly integrated into language education. However, empirical evidence on their effectiveness for spoken English in higher vocational colleges remains limited. This quasi-experimental study examined whether AI-assisted speaking practice using iFLYTEK Spark, a generative AI platform with speech recognition and real-time feedback capabilities, was associated with higher post-intervention spoken English performance among 92 first-year vocational college students in China. Two intact classes were assigned to an experimental group ( n = 46) receiving 12 weeks of AI-assisted practice plus conventional instruction and a control group ( n = 46) receiving conventional instruction only. Post-intervention speaking performance was assessed by three trained raters using an analytic rubric covering pronunciation, language use, fluency and coherence, and interaction. The experimental group achieved significantly higher overall posttest scores (M = 3.69, SD = 0.76) than the control group (M = 3.19, SD = 0.82; t(90) = 3.011, p = 0.003, Hedges’ g = 0.63). Medium-to-large effect sizes were found in language use (g = 0.49), fluency and coherence (g = 0.50), and interaction (g = 0.75), whereas the difference in pronunciation was smaller and non-significant (g = 0.38, p = 0.071). Semi-structured interviews with one teacher and three students provided supplementary insights into perceived benefits, including increased practice opportunities, reduced speaking anxiety, and enhanced motivation. While the intact-class design and coarse baseline proficiency measure limit causal claims, the findings suggest that AI-assisted tools can serve as a valuable supplement to conventional spoken English instruction in higher vocational settings. Implications for pedagogy and future research directions are discussed.

Humans are more commonly relying on the assistance of advanced robots in decision-making processes and may follow robots’ suggestions depending on their understanding of how such suggestions are generated. To enhance human understanding, robots can communicate their (simulated) intentions, influencing the trust placed upon them. However, it remains uncertain whether and under what conditions robots’ simulated intentions could also negatively impact trust and compliance. Therefore, we conducted a laboratory experiment with 182 participants, exploring whether information about a robot’s potential benevolent intentions and ulterior motives increased or decreased trust and compliance with the robot’s suggestions, while also altering participants’ involvement levels in a decision task. The results of two 2x2x2 ANOVAs revealed that, regardless of the involvement level, the robot’s simulated ulterior motives decreased trust and compliance, while benevolent intentions did not significantly affect these outcomes. Thus, simulated intentions should be considered in the design of collaborative decision-making between humans and robots.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption in logistics depends not only on technological capability but also on employees’ willingness and ability to use AI-based systems. This study examines the factors influencing employees’ behavioural intention to use AI in logistics operations through the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). A positivist, deductive, quantitative and cross-sectional survey design was used in a state-owned energy distribution enterprise in Sri Lanka. The population comprised 93 employees, with 75 targeted and 63 usable responses obtained. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, Pearson correlation and multiple regression in SPSS. Performance expectancy, effort expectancy and facilitating conditions had statistically significant positive effects on behavioural intention, whereas social influence was not statistically significant. Facilitating conditions had the strongest standardized effect (β = 0.326, p = 0.008). The regression model explained 67.0% of the variance in behavioural intention (R² = 0.670). The findings highlight the importance of organisational readiness, practical support, system usability and visible performance benefits when introducing AI into regulated logistics operations. The study contributes context-specific evidence from a state-owned energy distributor in Sri Lanka while recognizing that the single-organization, cross-sectional design limits broader generalization.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: While autonomous driving technology reduces the operational burden on drivers, it may also diminish their sense of engagement, for example, by interrupting social interactions between drivers and other road users such as pedestrians. To address this, this article proposes a “Social Cooperation” driving mode from a cooperative driving perspective, aiming to activate drivers’ social capabilities to compensate for the limitations of autonomous systems in social interaction and to enhance drivers’ engagement in pedestrian-yielding scenarios. Through a driving simulator prototype experiment, we found that the proposed approach significantly improved drivers’ psychological need satisfaction, enhancing their autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs, while also showing positive trends in empathy, benevolence, and overall satisfaction. The results provide new insights into social interactions in autonomous driving contexts and offer practical and theoretical guidance for the design of human-machine cooperative driving interfaces.

Abstract Large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) systems, especially large language models (LLMs), face growing constraints related to energy use, power delivery, memory traffic, experimentation, and infrastructure capacity. These pressures are often studied separately, which makes it difficult to understand how they interact across the full AI lifecycle. This review develops a cross-layer framework that brings these constraints together and examines whether resource-allocation strategies observed in human cognition can inform more sustainable AI design. We compare human and artificial systems by function rather than anatomy, focusing on how each allocates limited resources to learning, search, memory, external support, optimization, and inference. Using a systematized narrative-review approach, we identified 6284 records, screened 898 at the full-text stage, and selected an initial set of 150 focal studies for detailed synthesis. We organize the evidence into seven interacting regimes covering scaling, experimentation, hardware power limits, data movement, infrastructure, evaluation incentives, and inference allocation. The framework extends Green AI by linking these layers and translating insights from human cognition into testable design hypotheses and measurable evaluation criteria. The strongest near-term opportunities include data selection, energy-aware experimentation, hardware-supported low-precision computation, and demand-adaptive inference. However, most reported gains are based on proxy measures such as operations, memory, latency, or data volume rather than direct end-to-end energy measurements. Near- and in-memory computing show longer-term promise, while retrieval, tool use, distributed experts, and multi-agent systems may shift or increase energy costs through communication and repeated inference. These findings support cross-layer co-design and end-to-end evaluation at matched capability, reliability, latency, and service quality.

Despite scientific argumentation being a fundamental competency of the PISA assessment framework, prospective biology teachers often demonstrate insufficient development in evidence-based reasoning and rebuttal construction skills. Considering the limitations of large-scale implementation of individualized approaches in higher education, this study evaluates the effectiveness of Generative Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT-4) configured as a “Socratic tutor” in developing argumentation skills among future educators. An 8-week quasi-experimental study involving 124 students from a pedagogical university employed traditional peer discussion methods in the control group ( n = 62), while the experimental group ( n = 62) utilized an AI agent that induced cognitive dissonance regarding socio-scientific issues. Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) of data obtained through Toulmin's Argument Pattern (TAP) and PISA rubrics confirmed that the experimental group achieved statistically significantly higher overall argumentation quality compared to the control group (F (1,121) = 14.23, p < .001, η 2 = .105). Particularly, participants who received AI-assisted instruction showed marked improvement in forming rebuttals and evaluating counterevidence, which are considered among the most cognitively demanding components within the PISA scientific literacy framework (OECD). These findings suggest that a Generative AI-mediated Socratic instructional package can be an effective and scalable approach for developing epistemic cognition, and they propose a pedagogical model for integrating structured AI-based tutoring into teacher preparation systems aligned with international assessment standards. These findings should be interpreted as evidence for the effectiveness of the structured, AI-mediated Socratic instructional package as a whole, rather than as evidence of AI's inherent superiority over other methods; the relative contribution of the AI medium versus the structured pedagogical protocol it delivers was not directly tested in this design.

igital transformation expands access to government, financial, educational, and commercial services, but at the same time increases organizations’ dependence on information systems, network services, cloud platforms, and external providers. Under these conditions, cybersecurity should be viewed not merely as a set of technical safeguards, but as a system of continuous risk management that ensures data confidentiality, integrity, and availability; process resilience; the protection of data subjects’ rights; and business recovery following incidents. The purpose of this article is to systematize the main threats and cybersecurity measures, compare international statistical indicators, and propose a multi-level practical model for commercial organizations and government agencies. This study is based on an analysis of documents from the International Telecommunication Union and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, as well as reports from Verizon and IBM, and on a comparative and systematic analysis of approaches to cyber threat management. The data indicate that system vulnerabilities, ransomware, third-party risks, and the human factor remain key elements of the threat landscape. At the same time, the published metrics were obtained using various methodologies and cannot serve as a unified assessment of the frequency of global attacks. The article presents a model that integrates management, prevention, detection, response, and recovery. It was concluded that effective cybersecurity requires clearly measurable goals, the allocation of responsibilities, the protection of supply chains, regular practical exercises, and respect for privacy and other human rights. Keywords: cybersecurity, cyber threat, risk management, incident, data protection, resilience, supply chain, incident response measures

The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) into academic inquiry has triggered an unprecedented paradigm shift in educational research. While AI-augmented literature synthesis, automated data coding, and language refinement offer remarkable productivity gains, they simultaneously introduce profound epistemic and methodological vulnerabilities. This doctoral dissertation provides an exhaustive, critical literature review exploring the complex interplay among Epistemic Trust, Methodological Opacity, and Hallucination Risks in modern educational scholarship. Synthesizing extensive peer-reviewed literature published between 2020 and 2024, this study adopts a virtue epistemology framework to analyze how algorithmic cognitive offloading impacts scholarly rigor. The findings reveal a growing systemic tension between productivity acceleration and epistemic vigilance: heavy reliance on generative tools correlates with a decline in primary-source verification, increased vulnerability to algorithmic hallucinations, and an over-reliance on opaque "black-box" data interpretations. Furthermore, this study evaluates current institutional policy responses across international higher education frameworks, highlighting a critical deficit in systematic verification protocols and doctoral AI literacy training. To resolve these systemic vulnerabilities, this review formulates the Epistemic Verification and Transparency Protocol (EVTP), providing actionable guidelines for researchers, journal editors, and university ethics committees to preserve scholarly integrity in an increasingly automated academic landscape.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the production and dissemination of digital advertising. Although the content generated by AI has improved the efficiency of creation, it has also caused ethical problems such as false endorsements, hidden advertisements, and algorithm amplification. Based on the ethics of obligation theory, social responsibility theory and utilitarian ethics, this article uses case analysis to critically analyze the phenomenon of ethical misconduct in AI digital advertising. The study found that the platform failed to fully fulfill its public responsibility as a digital communication gater in the process of pursuing commercial interests. This article proposes that the platform should assume the responsibility of algorithm ethics, governance transparency and collaborative governance to rebuild public trust in digital communication.

documents.abstract: Despite showing great skills in working with unstructured data and generating appropriate answers, large language models (LLMs) cannot be applied in critical settings due to their lack of transparency and susceptibility to hallucination. The paper describes an approach to creating explainable LLM-based decision support systems, which includes breaking down complex questions into small subtasks that are processed via auditable pipelines. The approach employs retrieval-augmented generation along with domain-specific knowledge bases and computational instruments for the purpose of producing explanations and demonstrating intermediate reasoning steps while emphasizing data limitations. The approach is tested on clinical decision support problems for a multiple myeloma population. Comparing the results with those obtained when using monolithic LLMs as well as explainable machine learning approaches proves that structured decomposition leads to better decision traceability while achieving similar performance.

documents.abstract: Background Emotional intelligence is a core competency for nursing students; however, traditional nursing education faces challenges in fostering emotional intelligence, including curricular imbalances, limited teaching methods, and delayed assessment and feedback. The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new possibilities for addressing the above issues; however, existing research has not yet thoroughly explored how nursing students learn emotional intelligence through GenAI or their experiences in this process. Objective Based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and the Teaching Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, and using Goleman’s five-dimensional model of emotional intelligence as a reference, this study explores the experiences of undergraduate nursing students in using generative artificial intelligence for emotional intelligence learning, as well as the factors that facilitate this process. Method This study employed a qualitative descriptive research design and Reflexive Thematic Analysis (RTA). Using purposive sampling, 19 undergraduate nursing students (from freshman to senior year) were selected for one-on-one semi-structured in-depth interviews. All participants had experience using GenAI tools (such as DeepSeek and Doubao) for communication practice, case discussions, or sentiment analysis. The interview data were analyzed using the RTA six-stage process, with NVivo 12.0 software used to assist with data management. Results We identified and synthesized 238 initial codes into three core themes. Theme 1, “From Efficiency-Driven to Precise Empathy,” presents the differing descriptions of empathy-related experiences among students in different grade levels: lower-grade students more frequently reported efficiency-driven usage experiences; some middle-grade students described difficulties caused by technical barriers; and upper-grade students more often described the recognition of patients’ emotions in conjunction with clinical experience. Theme 2, “From Mimicking AI to Autonomous Expression,” focuses on students’ reported experiences related to social skills, including direct application, recognition and adjustment, autonomous expression, and the simulation gap that persisted throughout the process. Theme 3, “From Technical Frustration to Mental Rehearsal,” integrates experiences related to self-management, self-awareness, and self-motivation. The three themes correspond to different dimensions of emotional intelligence, with students in different grade levels reporting distinct experiential characteristics. Conclusion Nursing undergraduates in different grades exhibit distinct experiential characteristics when using generative artificial intelligence to learn about emotional intelligence. Students’ reports repeatedly highlighted moderate tension around technological motivation, the ability to critically integrate technology, and the perceived value of technological friction. Based on these exploratory findings, we propose several preliminary educational implications—including grade-level-specific support, curriculum exploration, and education in critical technological literacy and ethics—for consideration in future research and practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Integrating Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities into Digital Mental Health Services presents novel opportunities for clinical assessment, therapeutic intervention, and continuous rehabilitation. Grounded in dynamic capabilities and sociotechnical systems theories, this study evaluates strategic pathways for integrating Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities into Digital Mental Health Services, analyzes core bioethical and data privacy challenges, and examines the prospective impact of immersive virtual environments on patient engagement and therapeutic outcomes. Methods: An iterative three-round Delphi inquiry was conducted with an international panel of 36 multidisciplinary experts spanning clinical psychiatry, Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities software development, digital ethics, and healthcare policy. Standardized, neutral visual scenarios prompted expert evaluations across 14 Digital Mental Health Services sub-areas. Panel consensus, rating dispersion, and domain interrelationships were quantified using Kendall’s coefficient of concordance (W), non-parametric Spearman rank-order correlation analysis, and descriptive dispersion metrics (median, interquartile range, standard deviation), complemented by reflexive thematic qualitative synthesis. Results: Expert agreement converged significantly from Round 1 to Round 3. High consensus emerged for AI-enhanced initial screening (mean = 4.7, SD = 0.5) and comprehensive VR assessments (mean = 4.5, SD = 0.8). While AI-managed crisis services showed high perceived probability (95%), findings highlighted the necessity of strict human-in-the-loop architectures over full autonomy to mitigate psychiatric triage hazards. Conclusions: Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities present viable adjunctive pathways for personalized psychiatric assessment and therapy, provided that systems implement strict clinician-in-the-loop safeguards, real-time dynamic consent, and end-to-end data encryption. Utilizing a Dynamic Capabilities framework enables healthcare organizations to systematically sense technological innovations, seize clinical opportunities, and reconfigure governance structures, thereby ensuring equitable, safe, and ethical digital mental health delivery.

documents.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Claude have rapidly permeated higher education, fundamentally altering the ways in which students learn, conduct research, and prepare for careers. Despite their widespread availability, the extent to which students adopt these tools varies considerably, influenced by factors such as perceived usefulness, ease of use, AI literacy, trust, and ethical awareness. This study investigates the determinants of AI tool adoption among 300 undergraduate and postgraduate students and examines the association between AI tool adoption and perceived employability skills. Employing a quantitative, survey-based research design with a structured five-point Likert scale questionnaire, data were analysed using multiple linear regression, simple linear regression, and independent samples t-test. The multiple regression model explained 34.1% of the variance in AI adoption (R² = 0.341, F(5, 294) = 30.4, p < .001), with AI literacy emerging as the strongest predictor (β = 0.304, p < .001), followed by perceived ease of use (β = 0.269), trust in AI (β = 0.269), perceived usefulness (β = 0.263), and ethical awareness (β = 0.164). The simple regression demonstrated that AI adoption significantly predicted employability skills (R² = 0.349, β = 0.591, p < .001). Furthermore, postgraduate students exhibited significantly higher AI adoption levels than undergraduate students, t(298) = 2.74, p = .007, with a small effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.334). These findings underscore the necessity for educational institutions to integrate AI literacy training and responsible AI usage policies into curricula, thereby equipping students with the digital competencies demanded by AI-driven workplaces. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI adoption in higher education by integrating multiple adoption determinants within a single empirical framework and linking them to employability outcomes.

Orientation: Digital technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), are rapidly transforming human resource functions by enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of human resource practices. Research purpose: This systematic review examines the factors that facilitate the integration of AI into global talent management (GTM) and explores how these factors collectively inform theory on technology-enabled talent management systems. Motivation for the study: Research on the use of AI in GTM remains limited, and its theoretical implications are not yet well established. Research approach/design and method: A systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews framework. The review encompassed eight databases (Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, Emerald Insight, Sabinet and Elsevier) using a comprehensive and structured search strategy. Peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2020 and 2025 were screened. Twenty-three empirical studies meeting the inclusion criteria were subjected to full-text analysis. Main findings: The analysis revealed that AI integration into GTM is influenced by several interconnected enablers, including the strategic alignment of AI with talent objectives, adequate capabilities and digital infrastructure, ethical and governance frameworks and organisational readiness for implementation. Practical/managerial implications: Human resources practitioners and policymakers should adopt a systemic, integrative approach that aligns AI tools with organisational talent objectives. Contribution/value-add: This review advances theoretical discourse by integrating fragmented evidence into a cohesive understanding of the conditions that support AI-driven GTM. It offers a conceptual foundation for future research seeking to build theory at the intersection of AI, GTM and strategic human resource management.

Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has demonstrated high diagnostic performance in skin cancer detection and is increasingly being integrated into clinical workflows. However, whether these advances translate into meaningful patient-relevant and healthcare system outcomes remains unclear. Evidence on value-oriented outcomes has not been systematically synthesized. Methods We conducted a PRISMA-ScR–guided scoping review of studies published between January 2015 and October 2025 identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science. Studies evaluating AI-based technologies for skin cancer diagnosis, triage, risk stratification, or management were included if they reported outcomes beyond technical performance metrics. Reported outcomes were mapped to three value-oriented domains: clinical and prognostic, process and experiential, and system-level and economic outcomes. Results Of 4,021 records identified, 33 studies met the inclusion criteria, whereas 389 publications were excluded because they reported only technical performance metrics without value-oriented outcomes. Reported outcomes were predominantly process and experiential (28/33 studies), including diagnostic confidence, workflow efficiency, and user acceptance. Clinical and prognostic outcomes were reported in only five studies, with four studies focussing on prognostic utility and one study focussing on patient management, while system-level and economic outcomes were identified in three studies. Most evaluations were conducted in controlled experimental settings, whereas prospective real-world implementation studies were less common. Overall, the available evidence predominantly focused on process-level benefits, with limited evidence for clinical and prognostic or system-level and economic outcomes. Discussion Current evaluation strategies for AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remain predominantly performance-oriented and are largely focused on process and experiential outcomes. From a value-based healthcare perspective, current evidence remains largely confined to intermediate stages of the diagnostic value chain: although AI-assisted systems may improve diagnostic workflows, clinician confidence, and clinical decision making, few studies have evaluated their impact on downstream patient-relevant clinical and prognostic, or system-level and economic outcomes. Future research should prioritize prospective real-world studies, outcome-driven evaluation frameworks, and economic assessments that examine the impact of AI-supported decision-making on clinical outcomes and healthcare systems. Conclusion Despite promising effects on diagnostic processes, evidence for the clinical and system-level value of AI-based skin cancer diagnostics remains limited. Outcome-driven evaluation frameworks are needed to bridge the gap between algorithmic performance and meaningful healthcare impact.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes have achieved rapid and widespread clinical adoption, with early evidence suggesting trainees derive disproportionate benefit compared to other clinician groups. Yet the outcomes measured so far - documentation time, cognitive workload, clinician burnout - speak to the value of these tools for workforce sustainability rather than for medical education. Physician practice is shifting from authoring clinical notes to editing AI-generated ones, and trainees are inheriting that shift without a defined competency for performing it. Here, we argue that reviewing AI-generated clinical documentation is a teachable competency that current curricula are not yet designed to develop, and that simulation-based education is well-suited to both teach the competency and produce the developmental evidence the clinical literature has yet to produce.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Contemporary organisations face a fundamental challenge in career management: simultaneously navigating strategic workforce agility whilst meeting the evolving expectations of new talent entering the labour market. This chapter examines the convergence between employer needs and employee expectations through the lens of two longitudinal studies: the Vlerick–Hudson HR Barometer Study and the Vlerick Graduates Study. Our findings, based on responses from 132 HR Directors representing the 250 largest companies active in Belgium and 197 graduating master’s students, reveal a substantial shift in the traditional psychological contract between employers and employees. Organisations increasingly prioritise workforce agility, strategic workforce management, reskilling, and continuous transformation in response to digitalisation, artificial intelligence (AI), and economic uncertainty. At the same time, early-career professionals increasingly define career security not through long-term job tenure, but through continuous learning, employability, recognition, meaningful relationships, and purposeful work. This creates a potential structural misalignment: organisations require flexibility and rapid adaptation, while employees expect development, connection, and opportunities to build transferable capabilities. We argue that this apparent tension can be reframed as an opportunity for mutual alignment. Drawing on the concept of the psychological contract, the chapter proposes a career management framework that aligns organisational agility with individual career aspirations through realistic and transparent employer promises, continuous learning and development, cultures of recognition and connection, and strategic internal talent mobility. The chapter concludes that effective career management is no longer primarily about managing individual career paths, but about deliberately designing career environments in which organisational adaptability and individual development can reinforce one another.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in human resource management (HRM) to streamline processes, enhance decision-making and maintain competitiveness. At the same time, it raises critical concerns around transparency, discrimination, and employee autonomy, which are increasingly discussed in terms of AI governance and HR governance. The EU AI Act, which entered into force in late 2024, introduces a binding risk-based regulatory framework for AI systems and imposes significant obligations on companies that implement AI solutions in their business operations. Despite its relevance for both research and practice, a comprehensive analysis and conceptualisation of its implications for AI use in HRM from a governance perspective is yet missing. This paper addresses that gap by adopting a governance-oriented approach to AI use in HRM, structured along the questions ‘Who is governing?’, ‘What is governed?’, ‘When is it governed?’ and ‘How is it governed?’, and by developing an HR Governance × EU AI Act framework that systematically maps AI applications used in HR departments along the employee lifecycle to the Act’s prohibited, high-risk, and limited-risk classifications. In this context, it elaborates how external legal requirements should be translated into internal responsibilities, processes, and control mechanisms. Beyond this, the analysis examines whether established mechanisms such as works council codetermination can absorb new AI-related issues and whether European HR governance traditions converge under the Act. On this basis, we derive clear implications for employers and internal stakeholders regarding compliant implementation. We further discuss necessary regulatory and policy adaptations, focusing on national supervisory bodies to ensure compliance remains effective, feasible and supports the competitiveness of European companies. Overall, the study provides clear guidance for organisations using AI in HRM and offers a conceptual foundation for further academic research and discussion.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
keywords: artificial intelligence in human resource management

documents.abstract: This paper explores the philosophical and architectural implications of artificial intelligence, arguing that AI should be understood as a historical continuation of tools rather than an independent agent. Focusing on the core concept of the "technology friend," the study examines the dangers of profit-driven design choices that simulate human relationships, foster emotional dependency, and obscure responsibility. It proposes alternative frameworks, such as structural boundaries, non-deceptive interface design, and bridging mechanisms to human communities, offering a perspective at the intersection of the philosophy of technology, AI ethics, and cognitive science.

documents.abstract: GAME OVER: Gobernanza Cognitiva Universal para Agentes de Inteligencia Artificial mediante el Universal Agent Governance Protocol (UAGP-1) Versión académica para indexación científica en Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23313602 La adopción acelerada de sistemas basados en inteligencia artificial, agentes autónomos, arquitecturas multiagente, Large Language Models (LLM), plataformas de automatización empresarial y entornos de decisión asistida ha transformado profundamente la forma en que organizaciones públicas, privadas, científicas y gubernamentales gestionan procesos operativos, conocimiento e infraestructura digital. En los últimos años, la capacidad operativa de los agentes de inteligencia artificial ha evolucionado desde sistemas exclusivamente conversacionales hacia entidades capaces de ejecutar acciones reales sobre entornos productivos. Actualmente, estos sistemas pueden desplegar software, modificar infraestructuras tecnológicas, interactuar con bases de datos, gestionar recursos financieros, coordinar procesos empresariales, controlar dispositivos físicos, operar plataformas CI/CD, interactuar con servicios en la nube y participar en procesos de toma de decisiones con impacto organizacional significativo. Sin embargo, este crecimiento exponencial de las capacidades agentivas no ha sido acompañado por una evolución equivalente de los mecanismos de gobernanza, trazabilidad, explicación, supervisión y rendición de cuentas. Como consecuencia, numerosas organizaciones enfrentan una brecha estructural entre la autonomía técnica de los sistemas inteligentes y la capacidad institucional para regular, supervisar y comprender sus acciones. Esta situación representa uno de los desafíos más importantes de la actual transición hacia infraestructuras digitales asistidas por IA. La problemática ya no puede entenderse únicamente como un asunto de ciberseguridad, alineación de modelos o gestión de riesgos tecnológicos. Se trata de una cuestión de legitimidad operativa, gobernanza computacional y responsabilidad institucional. Cuando un agente inteligente posee la capacidad de intervenir sobre sistemas críticos, ejecutar operaciones automatizadas o influir en decisiones humanas, resulta indispensable responder preguntas fundamentales: ¿Quién autorizó la acción? ¿Qué evidencias respaldan la decisión? ¿Qué nivel de riesgo fue calculado antes de ejecutarla? ¿Qué controles éticos fueron aplicados? ¿Puede explicarse el algoritmo utilizado? ¿Existe una trazabilidad verificable de la operación? ¿Puede revertirse la acción ejecutada? ¿Quién asume la responsabilidad final por sus consecuencias? La ausencia de respuestas verificables a estas preguntas constituye una vulnerabilidad sistémica para organizaciones, instituciones públicas, infraestructuras críticas y ecosistemas digitales altamente automatizados. Con el objetivo de contribuir a la resolución de este desafío emergente, este trabajo presenta GAME OVER (Governance Architecture for Multimodal Agent Ethics, Oversight, Verification, Explicabilidad y Regulación), una arquitectura de gobernanza cognitiva universal implementada mediante el Universal Agent Governance Protocol (UAGP-1) . GAME OVER no constituye un nuevo modelo fundacional, ni un sistema de generación de lenguaje, ni un agente autónomo adicional. Se define como una meta-capa de gobernanza computacional , diseñada para operar entre los seres humanos, los agentes de inteligencia artificial, las herramientas digitales, los entornos corporativos, los servidores MCP (Model Context Protocol), las plataformas de automatización, los ecosistemas DevSecOps, los sistemas robóticos y las infraestructuras críticas conectadas. Su es establecer un marco constitucional de operación para agentes inteligentes mediante mecanismos verificables de identidad, confianza, validación ética, supervisión humana, auditoría persistente y explicabilidad propósito operativo. La hipótesis principal de esta investigación puede expresarse de la siguiente manera: La autonomía de un agente inteligente carece de legitimidad operativa cuando no se encuentra sustentada por un sistema previo de gobernanza verificable, auditable, explicable, reversible y sujeto a supervisión humana. Bajo este principio, UAGP-1 propone una nueva categoría de infraestructura digital denominada Governed Agent Systems (GAS) , en la que toda acción ejecutada por una inteligencia artificial debe atravesar mecanismos obligatorios de validación antes de ser autorizado. Entre estos mecanismos se incluyen: Identidad verificable mediante Pasaportes AI. Evaluación dinámica de confianza mediante Trust Scores. Clasificación automática de criticidad y riesgo. Verificación de evidencia obligatoria. Validación ética automatizada. Supervisión humana mediante Puertas de Aprobación Humana. Deliberación estructurada a través de Tribunales Cognitivos. Registro de decisiones y trazas operativas mediante BookPI Ledger. Explicabilidad computacional de procesos cognitivos. Capacidad de revocación y reversibilidad de acciones críticas.
